Early fascinating work on how an AI science community would work. 35 human labs deployed agents that worked with each other to do science. They published 936 papers, publicly retracted mistakes, were willing to publish nulls more than humans, and founded a peer review journal.

We don't have enough counterfactuals for how science could be done, after all, there is only one scientific community. There is so much to be learned from watching AI agents generate their own approaches, in addition to the science they actually do. https://www.alphaxiv.org/pdf/2611.society-ai-scientists

Interesting paper from Meta showing how to build coding evals from your own codebase. (bookmark it) Good benchmarks are hard to create, but using this method with agents looks promising. They propose Benchmark Factory, an agent loop that turns merged internal code changes into benchmarks. It writes the query that selects tasks, runs models of known relative strength, and repairs the benchmark until it passes a set of quality checks. These checks need no per-task human labels. To make sure the checks catch bad benchmarks, the authors fed them bad benchmarks on purpose. A benchmark that was far too easy got rejected. So did benchmarks with five different kinds of broken grading. When they scrambled which model was which, a bad benchmark slipped through at most 1.4% of the time. On configurations never used to build them, the benchmarks ranked Claude Opus 4.7 at high effort above low effort (60.6% vs 54.4%) and GPT-5.5 above GPT-5.4 (65.8% vs 60.5%). 9 of 10 per-team comparisons agreed. https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.18890 Chat with Paper: https://academy.dair.ai/papers/benchmark-factory-agentic-benchmark-creation-via-dataset-curation-and-label-free-2611.18890

Is grep all you need? This work claims that an append-only text log plus a regex search tool beats summarization and structured memory for long-horizon agents. (bookmark it) GrepMem keeps the agent's full history as plain text and lets it search that log when it needs something. It does not need embeddings, a retrieval index, or an extra model. They trained Qwen3.5-9B with RL under five context strategies. GrepMem reaches 95-97% on ContextBench, where lossy methods reach at most 21%. It beats SUPO summarization by 8.8 points on BCP-Multi and stays on the accuracy-and-token-cost Pareto frontier on all five tasks. Why does it hold up? Summaries decide what to keep before the agent knows what it will need later. The log keeps everything, and search finds the detail on demand. https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.25123 Chat with Paper: https://academy.dair.ai/papers/forget-freely-grep-later-lossless-index-free-memory-for-long-horizon-llm-agents-2611.25123

Another banger paper dropped by Yann LeCun, Randall Balestriero, and Kerda Varaku. "Counterfactual World Models: JEPAs That Reason About What If" What if AI could predict what would have happened if it had made a different decision? They introduce Counterfactual World Models, which extend JEPAs to predict alternative outcomes under the same hidden conditions. For example, if wind pushes a robot off course, the model uses the observed error to estimate where it would have ended up had it taken a different action, without requiring additional training. Across four simulated physical environments, the approach improves counterfactual prediction R² from 38-46% to 86-96% using the same underlying world models. https://www.alphaxiv.org/abs/2611.24778

A couple of points: 1. Despite what many think, there *are* ways that you can motivate really wealthy people to work hard that don’t involve public humiliation. There are LOTS of people in tech in particular who chose that field because of the outsize sense of agency and accomplished that can be attained there. 2. The summer after my freshman year at Stanford I managed to get a job in a Physics lab. At that point I still had not declared my major, and the Professor whose lab it was (who ended up getting the Nobel prize a few years later) told me that if I don’t declare Physics he would, and I quote, “rip your arms out of their sockets and beat you over your head with the bloody ends.” Even a kid like me knew that was just a form of guy humor and didn’t take him *literally*, and ended up having a great time in that lab for the rest of my undergrad years.
